claims.text: Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has relatively low hardness and strength because its simple solid-solution lattice lacks significant short-range chemical order and nanoscale precipitates.
The baseline CoCrFeNiTi lattice is near-ideal and chemically disordered.
Equimolar CoCrFeNiTi has minimal atomic-size mismatch.
Minimal atomic-size mismatch and the absence of local ordering produce a low barrier to dislocation glide.
A low barrier to dislocation glide gives CoCrFeNiTi high plasticity and machinability while lowering hardness and yield strength.
The starting material is an equimolar CoCrFeNiTi alloy in an as-cast or homogenized single-phase solid-solution state.
A minor compositional addition or moderate annealing treatment can promote localized chemical ordering or nanoscale precipitation.
Short-range order and fine precipitates serve as barriers to dislocation motion.
Homogeneous chemical distribution and minimal lattice distortion facilitate dislocation nucleation and motion in the starting alloy.
Chemically or thermally induced nanoscale ordering and precipitation pin dislocations and hinder glide.
Introducing nanoscale ordering or precipitation will increase hardness and yield strength relative to the unmodified alloy.
The predicted strengthening will likely be accompanied by decreased ductility.
TEM should detect nanoscale clusters or precipitates in successfully modified specimens.
The hypothesis is limited to 25–600 °C, comparable tensile or compressive loading rates, and conditions dominated by dislocation glide.
The hypothesis applies to relatively coarse-grained microstructures typical of as-cast or homogenized high-entropy alloys.
Grain size, minor impurities, and residual stresses may also influence the measured mechanical properties.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hardness and yield-strength increase despite identifiable nanoscale ordering or precipitation would falsify the proposed primary-mediator mechanism.
